To further assess the long-term adhesion of the PDMAA coating, a thin fluorescein-loaded hydrogel layer is first applied onto bulk Ecoflex to confirm the feasibility of hydrogel adhesion (Supplementary Fig.17). The same hydrogel is then successfully coated onto the microcatheter surface. Long-term adhesion and peel/abrasion resistance are evaluated by subjecting the hydrogel-coated microcatheter to 100 bending cycles in 0.9% saline at 37 °C. The bending primarily occurs in the soft microtube section. Following the bending test, the hydrogel coating is immersed in a fluorescent dye solution. As shown in Supplementary Fig.17, the fluorescence signals after bending verify that the hydrogel remained securely attached throughout bending, with no signs of significant peeling or abrasion.”
Comment 8: Magnetic safety – 150 mT static fields within 3–5 cm of the thoracic cavity warrant a discussion of pacemaker/ICD compatibility.
Response to Comment 8:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. While our magnetically controlled catheters show great potential in biopsy and payload delivery, their use in patients who have magnetic implants, such as cardiac pacemakers or implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), require careful planning due to safety concerns related to the interaction of these devices with magnetic fields. A clarification has been added in the Discussion section (Pages 20 and 21), as follows:
“While magnetically controlled catheters show great potential in biopsy and payload delivery, their use in patients who have magnetic implants, such as cardiac pacemakers or implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), require careful planning due to safety concerns related to the interaction of these devices with magnetic fields59.”
Comment 9: Serilisation and re-use – The assembly includes stainless-steel helix + silicone tube glued to a PE catheter. How does ethylene-oxide or plasma sterilisation affect the glue joint and magnetic remanence?
Response to comment 9:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important question regarding sterilisation. We conducted new experiments to evaluate the effect of ethylene oxide (EtO) sterilisation on the glue joint integrity and the magnetic remanence of the Helixoft system. A schematic of the test procedure is shown in Fig. R14. After sterilisation, the structure remains intact, and the magnetic remanence of the components is stable. We further confirm the structural integrity by performing a repeated bending test (n = 100 cycles) and payload delivery.
We have added the test procedure in Supplementary Fig. 15 of the Supplementary Information, and details of the sterilisation of the microcatheter have been added in the Methods section (Page 23), as follows:
“The microcatheter was sterilised using ethylene oxide (EtO). This sterilisation process did not affect its magnetisation or structural integrity, as verified by surface magnetic flux intensity measurements, repeated bending tests, and payload delivery performance (Supplementary Fig. 15).”
Fig. R 14 Sterilisation of the Helixoft-integrated microcatheter: a 1-mm-diameter device with biopsy needle and magnetic tubular tip, as well as a 300-μm microcatheter with a magnetic tubular tip. a, Schematic of the test procedure for evaluating the effects of sterilisation on structural integrity and magnetic remanence. b, Photograph of the sterilised and packaged devices. c, Results of structural integrity testing and surface magnetic flux density measurements.

Response to comment 10:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript, the stiffness states are now defined by helix pitch coverage length (L₁=turns×pitch) together with the corresponding bending stiffness (EI), thereby avoiding ambiguity related to catheter diameter. Specifically, for the helix with a pitch of 1 mm and diameter of 1 mm, the three states are: Low stiffness: (pitch coverage L₁= 0 mm, EI=2.06×10⁻⁸ N·m²), Medium stiffness:( pitch coverage L₁=3 mm, EI=3.60×10⁻⁸ N·m²), and High stiffness: (pitch coverage L₁ =6 mm, EI=1.72×10⁻⁷ N·m²). For the helix with a pitch of 0.2 mm and diameter of 1 mm, the three states are: Low stiffness: (pitch coverage L₁=0 mm, EI=1.72×10⁻9 N·m²), Medium stiffness:( pitch coverage L₁=1.9 mm, EI=9.72×10⁻9 N·m²), and High stiffness: (pitch coverage L₁ = 3.8 mm, EI= 7.43×10⁻8 N·m²).

Comment 12: 2. Provide a rigorous, quantitative benchmarking table that covers stiffness range, transition time, bending angle per Tesla, force throughput, and device OD across at least five state-of-the-art systems.
Response to comment 12:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion regarding the quantitative benchmarking table. As suggested, we have added a quantitative comparison table that covers stiffness range, transition time, bending angle per Tesla, force throughput, and device outer diameter (OD) across representative state-of-the-art systems (Table R1). We also summarise additional parameters, such as safety and remote controllability, and in vivo verification and quantitative safety assessment
The Helixoft system achieves an outer diameter of 300 µm, enabling application in narrow lumens (e.g., bronchioles, cerebral vasculature and fallopian tube). It employs a single-field decoupling strategy for stiffness tuning and steering via magnetic actuation, thereby ensuring safety and remote controllability. We validated the feasibility and safety of the system in pulmonary interventional procedures on three live porcine models, with quantitative safety assessments including navigation success rate, histological evaluation, and acute inflammatory response.
Comment 13: 3. Expand in-vivo validation to at least n = 3–5 large-animal procedures with histological assessment and device-specific adverse-event reporting.
Response to comment 13:
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment regarding the number of large-animal experiments and the importance of thorough safety evaluation. As shown in Figs. R6-R9 and the answer to Comment 3, we expanded the in vivo validation by performing two additional large-animal trials, resulting in a total of three trials (n = 3). We assessed the system’s efficacy through navigation success rates and drug delivery precision. We further evaluated safety, including mucosal trauma, acute inflammatory responses, and post-operative observation. Collectively, these results strengthen the evidence for both the efficacy and safety of the Helixoft system in vivo.

Comment 1: I am satisfied with the substantial improvements in the revised manuscript. The added model depth, inclusion of animal studies, and overall rigor represent a marked advance over the initial submission.
Response to comment 1:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the encouraging comments and for recognizing the improvements made in the revised manuscript. We truly appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment of the added model depth, inclusion of animal studies, and the overall enhancement in rigor.
Comment 2: However, the authors have not addressed my primary comment:
“Major comments
Limited conceptual novelty relative to prior art on magnetic, variable-stiffness catheters
The manuscript presents a helix-sliding sleeve that shortens/elongates a soft segment to achieve a 40-fold stiffness change, coupled with radial-magnet torque steering. Yet the key ingredients (i) a magnetically actuated rigid helix, (ii) sliding-sleeve stiffness modulation, and (iii) decoupled torque steering each appear in the literature individually or in combination. Representative examples include LMPA-based or SMP-based magnetic catheters with multi-segment stiffness switching (Chautems et al., 2020; Piskarev et al., 2023) as well as continuum robots that integrate ferromagnetic steering with mechanically programmable stiffness (Kim et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2024).
The manuscript, therefore, risks being seen as an incremental combination rather than a substantive advance.”
Response to comment 2:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point regarding the conceptual novelty of our work. To address this concern, we provide a detailed comparison between our Helixoft-integrated microcatheter system and previously reported magnetic catheters with stiffness-modulation capabilities in Table R1.
While these earlier studies each demonstrated distinct advantages, they also face significant limitations, particularly in terms of device miniaturization, operational safety, and remote controllability. For instance, LMPA-based or SMP-based magnetic catheters with multi-segment stiffness switching (Chautems et al., 2020;1 Piskarev et al., 20232 ) can achieve a broad stiffness modulation range (> 66-fold). However, their dependence on intense thermal or electrical stimuli raises safety concerns in delicate luminal environments, including potential material toxicity, thermal injury, and electrical damage. Moreover, the reported minimum outer diameters of these devices remain around 2.3 mm, as the intrinsic constraints of their actuation mechanisms hinder further miniaturization and integration at smaller scales. Similarly, concentric-tube-based stiffness-modulation catheters with continuous switching capability (Kim et al., 2019)3 face persistent challenges in downsizing due to the complex assembly of proximally controlled multilayer continuum tubes. The follow-the-leader catheter employing LMPA-based stiffness modulation (Mao et al., 2024)4 achieves periodic, tip-based elongation under programmable magnetic fields and enables autonomous shaping, yet the coaxial configuration of dual tubes results in device diameters of 3–4 mm, restricting their use in narrow lumens.
In contrast, the present Helixoft system is specifically designed for navigation within narrow and sensitive luminal environments (e.g., bronchioles, cerebral vasculature, and fallopian tubes) by miniaturizing the variable-stiffness catheter to 300 μm in diameter. Achieving tunable mechanical performance at the microscale remains a major challenge as miniaturization inherently conflicts with the complex structural requirements for stiffness tuning. Our microrobotic system addresses this challenge based on a previously underutilized mechanism that harnesses microscale helical motion at the component level to dynamically modulate the otherwise static mechanical properties of the overall structure under a magnetic field. Through a decoupling magnetic control strategy, independent remote tuning of stiffness and active steering is achieved by combining helical motion with torque-driven bending of individual microrobotic components. This mechanism eliminates the need for potentially harmful stimuli such as thermal, optical, or electrical inputs. Furthermore, repeated in vivo validations across different animal models, together with systematic safety evaluations, confirm both the feasibility and biocompatibility of the Helixoft system.
